name: Victor Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach PE and design technology at Foundry Lane Academy, a secondary school in a steel town where the works still employ about a thousand people. Mornings I'm on the field or in the sports hall, afternoons I'm in the workshop teaching kids to use a pillar drill without losing a finger. I use AI every day for lesson plans, risk assessments and the fixtures list. What wears me out is the paperwork for every trip and the fact that I've got two subjects' worth of marking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you doing for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented flat over a bike shop on Furnace Road, and I'm on lower pay because I'm not on the main teaching scale yet for design technology. Savings are about three weeks of rent, because I bought a second-hand van last year for the football club kit. I coach the under-fourteens on Saturdays for free. There's only one other secondary in town, and it doesn't have a PE vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, AI's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd tell the lads at football and the staffroom that it's still saving me two hours a week on paperwork. Online I'd share how I use it for risk assessments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for my job, PE was never going to be replaced by a chatbot. The money's the problem, three weeks in the bank and a van loan. AI being a damp squib doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and finally start the holiday sports camps I've been planning, for the Easter and summer holidays. Charge twenty pounds a day, aim for twenty kids, use the school field if the head agrees. And I'd stop eating out on Fridays until the van's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. Like half-time when you're one goal down, but you know you can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's stopping the sports camps right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, mostly, and nerves about money. The insurance is about three hundred pounds a year and I haven't got it spare. AI could do the bookings and the forms, which takes away the bit that put me off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the school let you use the field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if I paid a bit of rent and kept it clean. The head, Mr Osei, likes anything that brings families in. I'd offer him free places for the kids whose parents can't pay.

say: I'd say AI's a **good tool**, not a miracle.
I'd share how I use it for **risk assessments**.
think: **PE** was never going to be replaced by a chatbot.
Three weeks of savings and a **van loan** are the real problem.
do: Start **holiday sports camps** at twenty pounds a day.
Use AI for **camp bookings** and forms.
Stop eating out on **Fridays** until the van is paid off.
feel: **Restless**, like half-time one goal down but able to win.
S0.quote: PE was never going to be replaced by a chatbot.
fieldNote: Victor's **money pressure** is real, but he sees opportunity.
He'd use AI to remove the **paperwork barrier** to his own business.
He plans **free places** for poorer kids, a community instinct.

steps.text: Launch Easter sports camps on the school field
Use an AI tool for camp bookings and forms
Stop eating out on Fridays until the van is paid off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, and teachers who learn it will be fine. I'd say the market will sort out who's useful, and it's on each of us to make ourselves useful. I'd be the one showing staff how to do risk assessments in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a decent spot. PE and the workshop are hands-on, so the robots are years off, and I already use AI daily. What worries me is design technology classes being merged and the drawing and design side done on screens, which would cut my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the camps to every holiday and add after-school clubs, aiming for an extra five hundred a month by summer. I'd offer to train other teachers on AI for an allowance. And I'd save the camp money until I had two months of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but up for it. Like the start of a cup match away from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market will sort it out. What about colleagues it doesn't sort out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's harder, I'll admit. Mrs Hale in the office does the trips and the bookings, and she's been here thirty years. I'd want the school to retrain our office manager, not dump her, that's just decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your hours actually be cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few lessons a week of design technology, if they put the drawing side on software. That's about a fifth of my pay. The camps would need to cover that, which is why I'd move fast.

say: I'd say teachers who **learn AI** will be fine.
I'd say it's on each of us to make ourselves **useful**.
think: **Hands-on** PE and workshop work keeps robots years off.
Design technology **merging** could cut a fifth of his pay.
do: Run **camps** every holiday and add after-school clubs.
Train other teachers on **AI** for an allowance.
Save camp money until he has **two months** of rent.
feel: **Uneasy** but up for it, like an away cup match.
S1.quote: I'd want the school to retrain our office manager, not dump her, that's just decent.
fieldNote: Victor mixes **free-market** talk with real decency towards colleagues.
He expects to lose a **fifth of his pay** from design technology cuts.
He'd **move fast** on side income to cover the gap.

steps.text: Run sports camps every school holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast, and people need to get moving, not wait for the government. I'd tell my football lads to learn a trade and keep fit. I'd say it straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 the design and planning side of my job goes, and teaching theory goes. What's left is the field and the workshop, which is hands-on, so I've got until about 2031. That's three years. With three weeks of savings, three years is tight but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the sports business: camps, clubs, maybe a small gym for teenagers in a unit on the industrial estate. I'd use AI for all the admin so it's just me and the kids. I'd use the van as security for a small loan, which scares me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like taking a penalty, you know what to do but anything can happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan with three weeks of savings is risky. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because sitting still is riskier. If I wait, everyone else will be starting something too. Better to borrow five thousand now than be scrambling in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031 when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think parents want a robot coaching their kid at football. Parents want someone who shouts their kid's name, not a robot coaching football. That's my bet, anyway.

say: I'd tell people to **get moving**, not wait for government.
I'd tell my football lads to **learn a trade** and keep fit.
think: By 2028 the **design and theory** side of his job goes.
The **field and workshop** give him until about 2031.
do: Go **all in** on camps, clubs and a teen gym.
S2.quote: Parents want someone who shouts their kid's name, not a robot coaching football.
fieldNote: Victor bets on **personal coaching** being robot-proof.
He'd take a **loan** despite thin savings, seeing inaction as riskier.
The **robot gap** is his window to build a business.

steps.text: Open a teen gym in a unit on the industrial estate
Run AI software for all bookings and admin
Expand holiday camps into weekly after-school clubs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up, so use it. I'd tell people to pick something hands-on and build it now. I'd be upbeat at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years suits me. I'd be thirty-two, with a business running alongside teaching, and the robots don't come until 2034. My only real worry is getting the money together to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the camps and clubs over two years while still teaching full time. I'd save two months' rent first, then think about the gym. And I'd keep teaching PE as long as the school needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Like the first day of pre-season training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be working two jobs for years. Is that sustainable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a lad on his own, yes. I've got no kids, no partner to answer to, just a van and a whistle. If I'm going to graft, it's now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever want a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in time. My dad worked two jobs so we could have football boots. I'd want my kids to have that same example.

I'd tell people to build something **hands-on** now.

His only real worry is **start-up money**.
do: Build **camps and clubs** over two years while teaching.
Save **two months' rent** before the gym.
Keep teaching **PE** as long as needed.
S3.quote: My dad worked two jobs so we could have football boots.
fieldNote: Five years lets Victor **grow gradually** without a risky loan.
His **father's example** shapes his work ethic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who can't adapt in a decade isn't trying. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years looks good for me. I'd be thirty-seven, with a decade of AI skills and a sports business, and coaching won't see robots until 2039. I think I'd come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching, build the camps steadily, and open the teen gym by about 2030. I'd use AI for everything that isn't standing on a field. I'd want a family by then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Like a fixture list you know you can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who can't adapt isn't trying. What about people with less choice than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair, I was too harsh. Some people have kids and debts and nothing nearby. They'd need help, maybe apprenticeships paid by employers. But I'd still want them to help themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Injury, mostly. If I wreck my knee, the whole plan's in trouble. That and the steelworks closing, because then families can't pay for camps.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty to adapt.
I'd say it **kindly**, but I'd still tell people to start preparing now.
think: At **thirty-seven** he'd have AI skills and a sports business.
He's sure **coaching** won't see capable robots until about 2039, if ever.
do: Use AI for everything that isn't **on the field**.
S4.quote: If I wreck my knee, the whole plan's in trouble.
fieldNote: Victor expects to **come out ahead** with ten years.
He softens his **free-market** line when challenged.
His real risks are **injury** and the steelworks closing.

steps.text: Open the teen gym on the industrial estate by 2030
Use AI for all business admin

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to build anything before it hits. What would help is cheap start-up loans for people like me, and paid apprenticeships so lads from this town have something to aim at.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the steelworks. If the steelworks closes, the whole town changes, kids, families, everything. That matters more than AI round here.
